sections.minutes: sum of the subsection time boxes
sections.order_note: Teaching order follows one request: who sends it and how it is checked (1), what a policy says (2), how many policies decide (3), which identities hold keys (4), how a role replaces keys (5), how a service receives a role (6), what changes across accounts (7), third parties (8), employees (9), app users, servers and pipelines (10), conditions on an allow (11), ceilings for delegation (12), the one resource type that breaks the union (13), and how to find what to remove (14).

sections.heading: Every AWS call is a signed request that IAM answers

plan.problem: AWS receives millions of calls. For each one it must know who sent it and whether that sender may do it.
trace: Sign: the caller signs the request with its credentials; temporary credentials are an access key ID, a secret access key and a session token, and every call made with them includes the token (sts-temporary-credentials-include-session-token).
Authenticate: IAM provides [authentication and authorization] for AWS services (iam-faq-authentication-and-authorization): first who sent it.

Authorize: AWS evaluates the policies that apply, on every request (sts-temporary-credentials-cannot-be-revoked-permissions-can-change, display 'evaluated each time a request is made'). Point to the ladder iam-policy-gates here; the next subsection but one explains each rung.
Answer: the call runs, or an access denied error comes back; for an explicit deny the message says 'with an explicit deny in a <type> policy' (iam-access-denied-message-names-policy-type).
plan.table: Who secures what (shared responsibility, two or three rows): the hardware, software, networking and facilities that run AWS services: AWS (iam-shared-responsibility-security-of-versus-in-the-cloud); who can reach your data, set with IAM tools: you (iam-shared-responsibility-customer-applies-permissions-with-iam); classifying data and choosing encryption: you (same fact).
plan.why: Why check every call, not only the sign-in? Permissions change. Because AWS evaluates each request, a removed permission stops working for credentials that were already issued.
plan.exam_signal: "the customer is responsible for who can access the data" points to IAM permissions, the customer's side of the shared responsibility model (iam-shared-responsibility-customer-applies-permissions-with-iam).
plan.body_extras: One sentence: IAM is global; it has [a single endpoint in US East (N. Virginia)] and [the same role can be used in any Region]; a Region-restricting policy [makes IAM calls fail unless it exempts them] (iam-global-service-single-endpoint-us-east-1, iam-resources-global-same-role-any-region). If room: changes [can take some time] to replicate, so keep IAM changes out of critical code paths (iam-eventually-consistent-changes-replicate).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: AWS checks the policies on every call. The thing to watch is that an IAM change takes some time to replicate.
plan.stop_and_answer: A job runs with role credentials that expire in 50 minutes. An administrator removes s3:GetObject from the role's permissions policy. After the change replicates, does the job's next GetObject succeed? Answer: No; the credentials stay valid, but the policies are evaluated each time a request is made.
plan.pending: fr-0020 (what the request context holds: principal, action, resource, environment data). Do not write a sentence that lists the parts of the request context unless fr-0020 is filled when you write; 'the request names an action and a resource' as plain description is enough.

sections.heading: A policy statement pairs an effect with actions and resources

plan.problem: A permission must say exactly what is allowed, on what, and when. A policy is a JSON document with statements (iam-faq-policy-is-json-document).
trace: Effect: required, Allow or Deny (iam-policy-statement-required-elements).
Action: an Action or a NotAction element, for example s3:GetObject.
Resource: a Resource or a NotResource element, an ARN such as one bucket.
Condition: optional; the subsection on condition keys covers it.
Principal: only in a resource-based policy; you [cannot use the Principal element in an identity-based policy] (iam-principal-element-not-in-identity-policies).
plan.table: Three places a policy can live: AWS managed (AWS writes and updates it, you [cannot change the permissions of an AWS managed policy]); customer managed (you write it, attach it to many identities, IAM keeps [up to five versions]); inline (embedded in one identity, [a strict one-to-one relationship and is deleted with the identity]). Columns: Who writes it | Attach to many? | Versions. Facts: iam-aws-managed-policy-cannot-be-changed, iam-managed-vs-inline-policies, iam-policy-versions-five. Add one row note: resource-based policies are inline only (iam-resource-based-policies-inline-only).
plan.why: Why narrow an AWS managed policy? All customers can use it, so it [might not grant least-privilege permissions for your specific use cases] (iam-best-practice-aws-managed-policies-not-least-privilege). Least privilege means defining the actions on specific resources under specific conditions (iam-best-practice-least-privilege-definition).
plan.exam_signal: "developers need broad access but must not manage IAM" points to PowerUserAccess, which allows all services [except IAM, AWS Organizations and AWS Account Management] (iam-job-function-poweruseraccess-excludes-iam-org).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: a statement says allow or deny, which actions, on which resources. The thing to watch is a broad AWS managed policy.
plan.stop_and_answer: A customer managed policy already has five versions. A developer updates it with the AWS CLI and the call fails. What must the developer do first? Answer: delete an existing version that is not the default (iam-policy-versions-cli-must-delete-before-sixth); a rollback would set an older version as the default (iam-policy-versions-five).

sections.heading: AWS allows a request only when nothing denies and something allows
The root user and IAM users hold long-term credentials

plan.problem: Two kinds of identity keep credentials that work until a person removes them: the root user and IAM users.
trace: Root user: it has [full access by default] (iam-principals-have-no-permissions-by-default-root-has-full-access); it [must not be used for everyday tasks, even administrative ones] (iam-root-user-not-for-everyday-tasks-roles-instead); AWS says [do not create access keys for the root user] (iam-root-do-not-create-access-keys).

Root MFA: [All AWS account types (standalone, management, and member accounts)] require it, registered [within 35 days] (iam-root-mfa-required-all-account-types); three MFA types, passkeys and security keys recommended (iam-mfa-types-supported); [up to eight MFA devices] (iam-mfa-devices-up-to-eight).

IAM user: [IAM users have long-term credentials such as passwords and access keys] (iam-users-have-long-term-credentials-roles-do-not); [two access keys] so that rotation uses the second slot (iam-access-keys-max-two-per-user); the secret is [retrieved only at the time you create it] (iam-access-key-secret-shown-once).
Group: a policy on a group gives its permissions to every member (iam-groups-permissions-for-many-users); [groups cannot be nested] (iam-groups-no-nesting-not-principals).
plan.table: Columns: Identity | Long-term credentials | Use it for. Rows: root user | password, and access keys if someone creates them | the few tasks that only the root user can do (iam-root-tasks-only-root-can-do); IAM user | password and access keys | a tool that cannot use roles (iam-use-cases-that-still-need-user-access-keys); IAM role | none | everything else (iam-users-have-long-term-credentials-roles-do-not).
plan.why: Why push people to federation? AWS asks you to [Require your human users to use temporary credentials] (iam-best-practice-human-users-federate-with-identity-center): a stored password or key is a target that does not expire.
plan.exam_signal: "secure the root user" points to MFA on the root user and no root access keys (iam-best-practice-require-mfa-for-iam-and-root-users, iam-root-do-not-create-access-keys). Do not let the 2025 change decide anything here.
plan.go_deeper: Title: 'root access for member accounts'. At most 100 words: with AWS Organizations, AWS recommends [removing root user credentials from member accounts] (iam-root-centralized-root-access-member-accounts); new accounts then have [no root user credentials by default] (iam-root-central-access-deletes-member-credentials); a root-only task runs in [short-term privileged sessions] from the management account or a delegated administrator (iam-root-privileged-session-short-term-scoped, sts-assumeroot-callers). Cross-reference chapter 04 with an xref marker.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: give the root user MFA and lock it away. The thing to watch is an old access key that still works.
plan.stop_and_answer: An IAM user's console password expired yesterday. A script on the user's laptop calls AWS with the user's access key. Does the script still work? Answer: Yes; the user [can continue to use their access keys] (iam-password-expired-user-keeps-access-keys). Delete or deactivate the key.

sections.heading: A role gives temporary credentials to principals that its trust policy names
Passing a role to a service needs the PassRole permission

plan.problem: A developer who launches an instance chooses its role. If any role were allowed, the developer could give the instance more power than the developer has.
trace: Choose: the developer starts an EC2 instance or a Lambda function and names a role.
Check PassRole: the developer [must have the iam:PassRole permission for that role], and [PassRole only works with a service in the same AWS account] (iam-passrole-required-to-give-role-to-service).
Check trust: the role needs [a trust policy for the role that allows the service to assume the role] (same fact); a service principal [can't be "Service": "*"] (iam-principal-service-no-wildcard).

Deliver: the service assumes the role, and AWS delivers the temporary credentials to the compute resource (iam-compute-services-receive-role-credentials-no-keys-needed). On EC2 the console [creates an instance profile with the same name as the role] (iam-instance-profile-console-creates-same-name).
plan.table: Service role or service-linked role. Columns: Question | Service role | Service-linked role. Rows: who can edit it (an administrator can create, modify and delete it | you [can view but not edit its permissions]); permissions boundary (available | not available, iam-boundary-applies-to-users-and-roles-not-slr); limited by SCPs (yes | [Service-linked roles cannot be restricted by SCPs], iam-scp-no-effect-on-service-linked-roles). Facts: iam-service-role-vs-service-linked-role, iam-service-linked-role-owned-by-service.
plan.why: Why a separate permission to pass a role? Without it, a user could pass [a role that has more permissions than you want the user to have] (iam-passrole-prevents-privilege-escalation). Scope it with the Resource element and [the iam:PassedToService condition key].
plan.exam_signal: "developers launch instances but must not give them more permissions than approved" points to an iam:PassRole permission scoped to the approved roles (iam-passrole-prevents-privilege-escalation).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: to hand a role to a service, you need PassRole for that role. The thing to watch is PassRole on every role.
plan.stop_and_answer: An auditor searches AWS CloudTrail for the PassRole event of an instance that runs with an administrator role. What does the auditor find, and where should the auditor look instead? Answer: no PassRole event, because [PassRole is a permission, not an API call]; read the event of the call that launched the instance (iam-passrole-is-a-permission-not-api-call).
plan.pending: fr-0022 (the resource-based policy of a Lambda function that lets Amazon S3 or Amazon SNS invoke it). Write no sentence about it unless fr-0022 is filled when you write; then one sentence after the table: the execution role is for the function's own calls, and the function policy says who can invoke it.

sections.heading: Same-account access needs one allow but cross-account access needs two
An external ID stops the confused deputy in third-party roles

plan.problem: A monitoring vendor assumes a role in each customer's account. Another customer of the vendor could give the vendor your role ARN, and the vendor would act on your account. This is the confused deputy: [an entity without permission coerces a more privileged entity to act for it] (iam-external-id-prevents-confused-deputy).
trace: Vendor: gives each customer an ID [generated and controlled by the third party and unique per customer].
You: create a role whose trust policy names the vendor's account and adds [an sts:ExternalId condition in the role's trust policy].
Vendor: calls AssumeRole with your role ARN and your external ID.
AWS STS: the caller must be a principal in the trust policy and send the correct external ID, or the call fails (same fact).
plan.table: Columns: Who calls AssumeRole | External ID sent | Result. Rows: the vendor, for you | yours | Allow; the vendor, tricked by another customer | that customer's ID | Denied; an account that the trust policy does not name | any | Denied.
plan.why: Why is the ID not a secret? It does not prove identity; it ties each request to one customer. [AWS does not treat the external ID as a secret] and [anyone with permission to view the role can see it] (iam-external-id-is-not-a-secret).
plan.exam_signal: "a third-party company needs access to resources in the company's AWS account" with "MOST secure" points to a cross-account role with [an sts:ExternalId condition in the role's trust policy] (iam-external-id-prevents-confused-deputy).
plan.body_extras: Optional, if room: you [cannot switch to a role that requires an ExternalId in the AWS Management Console] (iam-external-id-role-not-switchable-in-console).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: add an external ID condition to the vendor's role. The thing to watch is that the external ID is not a secret.
plan.stop_and_answer: A vendor asks each customer to choose its own external ID. Two customers choose the value "prod". Which risk comes back? Answer: the confused deputy; the ID must be generated and controlled by the vendor and unique per customer (iam-external-id-prevents-confused-deputy).

sections.heading: IAM Identity Center gives employees one sign-in for many accounts
sections.xref: 05 (IAM Identity Center, Directory Service and Cognito) teaches the identity sources, Active Directory and Cognito federation in depth; here teach only the path from one sign-in to a role session.

plan.problem: Employees work in many accounts. An IAM user in each account means many passwords and keys to manage and remove.
trace: Sign in: the employee signs in once with the identity source, which can be Identity Center's own store or an existing one such as Microsoft Active Directory or Okta (iam-idc-identity-sources).
Assign: an administrator assigns a user or group a permission set for an account; a permission set is [a collection of permissions] (iam-idc-permission-sets).
Create roles: Identity Center [creates and manages IAM roles in individual AWS accounts for each permission set] (iam-idc-creates-role-per-permission-set).
Session: the employee gets a role session for the console or the AWS CLI; its length [uses the session duration setting on the permission set] (iam-idc-cli-and-console-use-permission-set-duration).
plan.table: Columns: Option | Where people sign in | Long-term credentials in each account. Rows: IAM users in each account | each account | yes (iam-users-have-long-term-credentials-roles-do-not); IAM federation with SAML or OIDC | an identity provider, linked to [specific AWS accounts] | no (iam-federation-with-iam-per-account-saml-or-oidc); IAM Identity Center | one portal for all accounts | no; it [does not create IAM users and groups] (iam-idc-no-iam-users-own-identity-store).
plan.why: Why roles underneath? Identity Center is [built on top of AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)] (iam-idc-built-on-iam-for-multi-account-access), so every session is a role session and the policy rules of this chapter still apply.
plan.exam_signal: "employees sign in with their existing Active Directory credentials to many AWS accounts" points to IAM Identity Center, connected through AD Connector or an AWS Managed Microsoft AD trust (iam-idc-on-premises-ad-two-options). It needs AWS Organizations with all features (iam-idc-accounts-need-organizations-all-features).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: one sign-in, then a role session in each account. The thing to watch is that it needs AWS Organizations with all features.
plan.stop_and_answer: A company connects Okta to IAM Identity Center. A second team wants to sign in with the company's Active Directory at the same time. Can Identity Center use both sources? Answer: No; it connects [only one directory or one SAML 2.0 identity provider] at a time (iam-idc-one-identity-source-at-a-time).

sections.heading: Cognito and Roles Anywhere give app users and servers temporary credentials
sections.xref: 05 owns Cognito user pools and identity pools in depth; one row each here.

plan.problem: Not every caller is an employee or code on AWS. App users, servers in a data center and build pipelines also call AWS, and none of them should hold a long-term key.
trace: App user: signs in with a Cognito user pool; a Cognito identity pool [deliver temporary IAM credentials] (iam-federation-cognito-identity-pools-deliver-iam-credentials). Use the display that fits the sentence.

Server outside AWS: presents an X.509 certificate from your own PKI to IAM Roles Anywhere and gets temporary credentials for a role; Roles Anywhere [requires PKI, the ability to issue and manage certificates] (iam-roles-anywhere-for-on-premises-and-hybrid-workloads, iam-best-practice-workloads-outside-aws-temporary-credentials).
Pipeline: a tool such as GitHub Actions [exchanges it for temporary AWS credentials that map to an IAM role] (iam-federation-oidc-jwt-exchanged-for-role-credentials).
plan.table: Columns: Who needs credentials | Use | What it exchanges. Rows: code on EC2 or Lambda | IAM role | nothing; AWS delivers the credentials (iam-decision-guide-workloads-assume-roles-with-temporary-credentials); an employee | IAM Identity Center | a sign-in; a user of your app | Amazon Cognito | a token (iam-decision-guide-cognito-for-own-application-auth); a server outside AWS | IAM Roles Anywhere | a certificate; a CI/CD pipeline | OIDC federation | a JSON Web Token.
plan.why: Why exchange instead of store? Temporary credentials mean you [do not have to distribute or embed long-term credentials in an application] (sts-temporary-credentials-advantages).
plan.exam_signal: "users of a mobile app upload files directly to Amazon S3" points to a Cognito identity pool, because it [deliver temporary IAM credentials] to app users (iam-federation-cognito-identity-pools-deliver-iam-credentials); AWS points mobile and browser apps to [Amazon Cognito or AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity], not to GetFederationToken (sts-getfederationtoken-long-term-user-credentials).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: exchange a token or a certificate for a role session. The thing to watch is that Roles Anywhere needs your own certificate authority.
plan.stop_and_answer: A build pipeline on GitHub Actions deploys to AWS with an IAM user's access key stored as a pipeline secret. Which change removes the stored key? Answer: OIDC federation; the pipeline exchanges its JSON Web Token for role credentials, so [no long-term credentials are embedded in the application] (iam-federation-oidc-jwt-exchanged-for-role-credentials).
plan.note: Cognito user pools are [not a supported identity source in IAM Identity Center] (iam-idc-cognito-not-an-identity-source): one sentence, only if room.

sections.heading: Condition keys narrow an allow to the right organization or network

plan.problem: An allow is often right only for some callers: your organization, your network, an encrypted connection, a person who used MFA.
trace: AWS reads the condition keys of the request.
It compares each key in the Condition element with the value in the policy.
A missing key makes [the condition is false] (iam-condition-missing-key-is-false-except-ifexists), so an Allow with that condition does not apply.
If every condition matches, the statement applies.
plan.table: Columns: The stem says | Condition key | Fact. Rows: only accounts in our organization | aws:PrincipalOrgID (iam-condition-key-principalorgid); only through our VPC endpoint | aws:SourceVpce (iam-condition-key-sourcevpce-sourcevpc); only over TLS | aws:SecureTransport (iam-condition-key-securetransport); only after MFA | aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent (iam-mfa-condition-key-multifactorauthpresent); only in approved Regions | aws:RequestedRegion (iam-condition-key-requestedregion; in an SCP, chapter 04).
plan.why: Why a condition instead of a list of accounts? With aws:PrincipalOrgID, policies [automatically include the correct accounts] when accounts join or leave (iam-condition-key-principalorgid).
plan.exam_signal: "only accounts in the company's organization can read the bucket" with "LEAST operational overhead" points to aws:PrincipalOrgID in the bucket policy (iam-condition-key-principalorgid).
plan.spot_the_bug: A team adds a bucket policy statement with Effect Deny, Principal *, Action s3:*, and Condition NotIpAddress aws:SourceIp 203.0.113.0/24 (the office range). Instances in private subnets reach the bucket through a gateway endpoint. What is wrong? Answer: through a VPC endpoint aws:SourceIp [can only be used for public IP address ranges] and is not available (iam-condition-key-sourceip-public-only-not-via-vpce); a missing key makes a negated operator true (iam-condition-missing-key-is-false-except-ifexists), so the Deny blocks the instances. Allow the endpoint with aws:SourceVpce. Put the JSON in a code block (code is not counted).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: add a condition key to the allow. The thing to watch is a key that the request does not carry.
plan.stop_and_answer: A bucket policy allows s3:DeleteObject only when aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is true. A script deletes with an IAM user's long-term access key. Can it delete? Answer: No; [long-term access keys do not include it] (iam-mfa-condition-key-multifactorauthpresent), so the condition is false and nothing allows the delete.
plan.note: No Go deeper here (file budget). ABAC and the data perimeter get at most one sentence, only if room: a data perimeter makes sure [only trusted identities access trusted resources from expected networks] (iam-data-perimeter-definition).

sections.heading: A permissions boundary lets developers create roles without escalating

plan.problem: Developers must create roles for their own workloads. A developer who can create any role can create an administrator role.
trace: Set the ceiling: an administrator writes a managed policy that holds the most that any workload needs; AWS says [use *permissions boundaries* to set the maximum permissions that you delegate] (iam-best-practice-boundaries-delegate-role-creation). Check the display matches the fact card exactly.
Attach: the boundary is set on the user or role ([an IAM entity, which is a user or role], iam-boundary-applies-to-users-and-roles-not-slr).
Grant: the developer's identity-based policy for the role grants what the workload needs.
Evaluate: the role can do only what is [allowed by both its identity-based policies and its permissions boundaries] (iam-permissions-boundary-sets-maximum-does-not-grant).
plan.table: Truth table, one action, no deny: Identity-based policy | Boundary | Result. Rows: allows s3:GetObject | allows s3 reads | Allow; allows s3:PutObject | allows s3 reads | Implicit deny; silent | allows s3:* | Implicit deny ([does not provide permissions on its own], iam-boundary-limits-but-never-grants); allows | denies | Explicit deny ([an explicit deny in either overrides the allow]).
plan.why: Why a ceiling instead of a review of every role? The administrator sets the maximum once, and developers move without waiting.
plan.exam_signal: "developers create IAM roles but must not grant more than a set maximum" points to a permissions boundary (iam-best-practice-boundaries-delegate-role-creation); "every principal of the account" points to an SCP instead (iam-scp-applies-to-member-root-user).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: a boundary caps what a role can ever do. The thing to watch is that it grants nothing by itself.
plan.stop_and_answer: A role's boundary allows dynamodb:*. Its identity-based policy allows s3:GetObject and nothing else. Can the role read a DynamoDB table? Answer: No; the boundary grants nothing, and no identity-based policy allows the read (iam-permissions-boundary-sets-maximum-does-not-grant).
plan.pending: fr-0021 (the iam:PermissionsBoundary condition key that forces developers to attach the boundary). Do not name the condition key or claim that IAM can require the boundary unless fr-0021 is filled when you write.

sections.heading: A KMS key policy decides whether IAM policies count for the key
sections.xref: 06 (KMS and CloudHSM) owns KMS: key types, rotation, multi-Region keys, envelope encryption and grants in depth. Teach here only how a key policy and IAM policies combine. Add <!-- xref: 06 KMS key policies --> once.

plan.problem: In one account, one allow is usually enough. A KMS key is the exception: an IAM allow alone may do nothing.
trace: Key policy: [every KMS key must have exactly one key policy], and it is [the primary way to control access] (iam-kms-key-policy-required-primary-control).
IAM policies: [IAM policies cannot allow access to a KMS key] unless the key policy allows it; [the default key policy enables IAM policies] (iam-kms-iam-policy-needs-key-policy-permission).
No exception for the root user: [not even the account root user or the key creator] has access without an allow (iam-kms-no-principal-has-access-unless-allowed).

Across accounts: [the key policy must give the external account permission], and IAM policies there must pass it on; [neither policy alone is sufficient] (iam-kms-cross-account-key-policy-and-iam-policy).
plan.table: Columns: Key policy | IAM policy | Result. Rows: enables IAM policies (default) | allows kms:Decrypt | Allow; does not enable IAM policies and does not name the role | allows kms:Decrypt | Implicit deny; names the role directly | silent | Allow; other account: names the account | allows in that account | Allow; other account: names the account | silent | Implicit deny.
plan.why: Why does the key policy decide? The key protects the data, so its owner must say yes in the key policy itself.
plan.exam_signal: "the role has kms:Decrypt in its IAM policy but still gets an access denied error" points to the key policy (iam-kms-iam-policy-needs-key-policy-permission).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: the key policy decides first. The thing to watch is a key in another account, which needs both policies.
plan.stop_and_answer: A role reads an SSE-KMS object from a bucket in its own account. The bucket policy allows the read. The role's IAM policy allows kms:Decrypt, but the key policy does not enable IAM policies. Does the read succeed? Answer: No; Amazon S3 calls AWS KMS with the caller's permissions (iam-forward-access-sessions-check-caller-permissions), and the IAM allow does not count for this key.
plan.note: Grants: one sentence at most, that AWS services that encrypt data [create a grant, use it, and retire it] (iam-kms-grants-used-by-services); details in chapter 06.

sections.heading: Access Analyzer and last-accessed data find permissions to remove

plan.problem: Permissions grow, and nobody remembers why. AWS says to start broad and [refine permissions to grant only the permissions required] (iam-faq-least-privilege-refine-as-use-cases-mature). Refining needs evidence.
trace: Set: generate a policy from what a role did; Access Analyzer can [analyze your CloudTrail logs] and [generate an IAM policy based on that activity] (iam-access-analyzer-policy-generation-from-cloudtrail).

Verify: policy validation checks [against IAM policy grammar and AWS best practices] (iam-access-analyzer-policy-validation); custom checks run in pipelines [such as their CI/CD pipelines] (iam-faq-access-analyzer-custom-checks-in-cicd).

Watch outside access: an external access analyzer [generates a finding for resources that allow public or cross-account access] (iam-access-analyzer-continuous-public-cross-account-findings), measured against the zone of trust (iam-access-analyzer-zone-of-trust).

Refine: unused access findings list [unused roles, unused access keys and unused passwords] (iam-access-analyzer-unused-access-findings); last accessed information on the [Access Advisor] tab shows services not used (iam-last-accessed-access-advisor-tab, iam-best-practice-last-accessed-remove-unused).
plan.table: Columns: The question | Tool. Rows: who outside the account can reach this bucket? | external access analyzer; which permissions does this role not use? | unused access analyzer or last accessed information; what policy does this application need? | policy generation; which users have passwords, keys and MFA? | credential report (iam-credential-report-contents); would this request be allowed? | policy simulator, which [does not make an actual AWS service request] (iam-policy-simulator-no-real-request).
plan.why: Why look at use instead of guessing? A permission that nobody used for months is a permission that an attacker can use and the team does not need.
plan.exam_signal: "identify resources that are shared with an external entity" points to IAM Access Analyzer (iam-access-analyzer-continuous-public-cross-account-findings); "remove permissions that are not used" points to unused access findings or last accessed information (iam-access-analyzer-unused-access-findings).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: Access Analyzer shows what is open and what is unused. The thing to watch is that external analysis works per Region.
plan.stop_and_answer: A company creates an external access analyzer in us-east-1 only. A bucket in us-west-2 allows public reads. Does the analyzer report it? Answer: No; it [analyzes only policies of resources in the Region where it is enabled] (iam-access-analyzer-external-is-regional). Unused access is different: [findings for the analyzer do not change based on Region] (iam-access-analyzer-unused-not-per-region).
plan.note: If room, one sentence: last accessed data counts [not just the successful attempts] (iam-last-accessed-counts-denied-attempts). The simulator [does not support resource control policies (RCPs)] (iam-policy-simulator-scps-yes-rcps-no) only if room.

traps.belief: If one policy allows an action, the request succeeds.
traps.truth: An explicit deny overrides an explicit allow.
traps.placed_in: 1-fast.md#signals-and-traps

traps.belief: An SCP or a permissions boundary that allows a service gives access to it.
traps.truth: Neither grants permissions; both set a ceiling.
traps.placed_in: 1-fast.md#signals-and-traps

traps.belief: A role with AdministratorAccess, or the root user, can do everything in a member account.
traps.truth: Effective permissions are the intersection of the SCP and the IAM policies, and an SCP also limits the member account's root user.
traps.placed_in: 1-fast.md#signals-and-traps

traps.belief: Code on an EC2 instance needs an access key in a file or a variable.
traps.truth: AWS delivers the temporary credentials of a role to the compute resource.
traps.placed_in: 2-deep.md#passing-a-role-to-a-service-needs-the-passrole-permission (Exam trap callout)

traps.belief: Across accounts, one side is enough: a bucket policy or a trust policy that names the other account.
traps.truth: Cross-account requests need an allow in both accounts; for a role, the caller's own policy also allows sts:AssumeRole.
traps.placed_in: 1-fast.md#signals-and-traps

traps.belief: A user who assumes a role keeps the user's permissions and adds the role's.
traps.truth: The permissions are not cumulative.
traps.placed_in: 1-fast.md#signals-and-traps

traps.belief: A role has its own password or access key.
traps.truth: A role has no standard long-term credentials.
traps.placed_in: 2-deep.md#iam-identity-center-gives-employees-one-sign-in-for-many-accounts (Exam trap callout: the employee's password stays in the identity source; in each account a role gives a session)

traps.belief: A bucket policy can name an IAM group as its principal.
traps.truth: You cannot identify a user group as a principal.
traps.placed_in: 2-deep.md#a-policy-statement-pairs-an-effect-with-actions-and-resources (Exam trap callout; the frozen Spot the bug in the cross-account subsection shows the same rule in a policy)

traps.belief: You can revoke one leaked set of temporary credentials directly.
traps.truth: One set cannot be revoked; revoking the role's active sessions denies every credential issued before that time.
traps.placed_in: 2-deep.md#every-aws-call-is-a-signed-request-that-iam-answers (Exam trap callout)

traps.belief: A permissions boundary on every user and role also limits the root user.
traps.truth: You cannot set a permissions boundary for the root user; an SCP reaches it in a member account.
traps.placed_in: 2-deep.md#a-permissions-boundary-lets-developers-create-roles-without-escalating (Exam trap callout)

traps.belief: The trust policy decides what a role session can do.
traps.truth: The trust policy names who can assume the role; the permissions policy decides what the session can do.
traps.placed_in: 2-deep.md#an-external-id-stops-the-confused-deputy-in-third-party-roles (Exam trap callout: the external ID in the trust policy decides who gets in, not what the vendor can do)

traps.belief: A wildcard principal in a bucket policy means the other account.
traps.truth: A wildcard principal with Allow grants access to all users, including anonymous users.
traps.placed_in: 2-deep.md#condition-keys-narrow-an-allow-to-the-right-organization-or-network (Exam trap callout)

traps.belief: The root user is the right identity for daily administration.
traps.truth: The root user must not be used for everyday tasks.
traps.placed_in: 2-deep.md#the-root-user-and-iam-users-hold-long-term-credentials (Exam trap callout)

traps.belief: IAM users with passwords or access keys are a good way to give employees, developers or a vendor access to AWS accounts.
traps.truth: IAM users have long-term credentials that stay valid until you revoke them; a role gives temporary credentials, and IAM Identity Center is the primary tool for workforce access.
traps.placed_in: questions only (added by traps-03 on 2026-10-12 for rule Q205; no hand-file marker yet)

traps.belief: An instance profile and IAM Roles Anywhere fit the same servers, so either one gives role credentials to EC2 instances and to servers in a data center.
traps.truth: An instance profile passes a role to an EC2 instance; IAM Roles Anywhere gives temporary credentials to on-premises and hybrid workloads and needs a PKI.
traps.placed_in: questions only (added by traps-03 on 2026-10-12 for rule Q205; no hand-file marker yet)

traps.belief: Amazon Cognito and IAM Identity Center serve the same users, so either one fits employees or the customers of an app.
traps.truth: IAM Identity Center is the primary tool for workforce access; Amazon Cognito manages identities for customer-facing applications.
traps.placed_in: questions only (added by traps-03 on 2026-10-12 for rule Q205; no hand-file marker yet)

traps.belief: An IAM policy or a bucket policy can give a role the use of a KMS key, whatever the key policy says.
traps.truth: The key policy is the primary control: unless it allows it, IAM policies cannot allow access to the key, and AWS KMS checks the caller's own permissions when Amazon S3 decrypts an object.
traps.placed_in: questions only (added by traps-03 on 2026-10-12 for rule Q205; no hand-file marker yet)

traps.belief: The IAM credential report or the IAM policy simulator shows which actions a role really used or which resources are shared.
traps.truth: The credential report lists users and the status of their credentials, and the simulator makes no real request; IAM Access Analyzer reads CloudTrail activity and resource-based policies.
traps.placed_in: questions only (added by traps-03 on 2026-10-12 for rule Q205; no hand-file marker yet)

traps.belief: For a managed service such as Amazon S3 or DynamoDB, the customer patches the hosts and the platform and protects the facilities.
traps.truth: AWS runs the infrastructure, operating system and platform of abstracted services and secures the facilities; the customer manages its data and applies IAM permissions.
traps.placed_in: questions only (added by traps-03 on 2026-10-12 for rule Q205; no hand-file marker yet)

traps.belief: To use an on-premises Active Directory with IAM Identity Center, you must run AWS Managed Microsoft AD with a trust to the domain.
traps.truth: AD Connector redirects requests to the on-premises directory without caching information in the cloud; a trust with AWS Managed Microsoft AD is the other option.
traps.placed_in: questions only (added by traps-03 on 2026-10-12 for rule Q205; no hand-file marker yet)

traps.belief: An MFA device registered to an IAM user protects the user's API calls by itself, through S3 MFA Delete or the user's access keys.
traps.truth: S3 MFA Delete cannot be applied to an IAM user, and long-term access keys carry no MFA status; MFA protection for API calls needs temporary credentials from GetSessionToken or AssumeRole.
traps.placed_in: questions only (added by traps-03 on 2026-10-12 for rule Q205; no hand-file marker yet)

traps.belief: The customer chooses the external ID, and one value can serve every vendor.
traps.truth: The external ID is generated and controlled by the third party and is unique for each customer.
traps.placed_in: questions only (added by traps-03 on 2026-10-12 for rule Q205; no hand-file marker yet)

traps.belief: One external access analyzer covers the resources in every Region.
traps.truth: An external access analyzer analyzes only the resources in its own Region, so you create one in each Region that you use.
traps.placed_in: questions only (added by traps-03 on 2026-10-12 for rule Q205; no hand-file marker yet)

question_slots.note: A role has an AWS managed policy that allows Amazon S3 actions and a customer managed policy with a Deny for s3:PutObject on one prefix; uploads to that prefix fail with an access denied error. Key: remove or narrow the Deny statement. Distractors: attach AdministratorAccess (trap: an allow cannot beat the deny), add a bucket policy allow, raise the permissions boundary. State in the stem that no SCP or boundary applies.

Qualifier none (difficulty 1). Which action secures the root user: turn on MFA for the root user, keep no root access keys, and use other identities for daily work. Decide the key with iam-best-practice-require-mfa-for-iam-and-root-users and iam-root-user-not-for-everyday-tasks-roles-instead, not with the 2025 change fact (volatile).

question_slots.misconception: AWS decides who in the customer's company can read the customer's data.
question_slots.note: Qualifier none. A company stores data in Amazon S3 and DynamoDB; which task is the company's own: setting IAM permissions (iam-shared-responsibility-customer-applies-permissions-with-iam). Distractors: patching the storage hosts, protecting the facilities, running the platform software (AWS side, iam-shared-responsibility-security-of-versus-in-the-cloud).

question_slots.misconception: An IAM user in each account is the simplest way to give employees access to many accounts.
question_slots.note: Many accounts in AWS Organizations, employees in the Identity Center identity store; centrally manage access. Key: IAM Identity Center with permission sets. Distractors: IAM users in each account (violates-qualifier), IAM users in one account that assume roles, Amazon Cognito user pool (sibling-confusion).

question_slots.misconception: To use on-premises Active Directory with AWS, you copy the users into IAM.
question_slots.note: On-premises Active Directory, many accounts, no user data cached in the cloud. Key: IAM Identity Center with AD Connector (iam-idc-on-premises-ad-two-options, 'without caching any information in the cloud'). Distractors: AWS Managed Microsoft AD trust (works, but the stem forbids a directory in AWS), IAM users synchronized by a script, Cognito.

question_slots.misconception: A mobile app needs an access key embedded in the app to upload to Amazon S3.
question_slots.note: Mobile app users upload photos directly to S3 with temporary credentials. Key: Cognito identity pool (iam-federation-cognito-identity-pools-deliver-iam-credentials). Distractors: IAM Identity Center (sibling-confusion), an IAM user key in the app, GetFederationToken from the app (sts-getfederationtoken-long-term-user-credentials).

Select TWO, five options. A monitoring vendor needs read access to the company's account. Keys: create a role that trusts the vendor's account and has a read-only permissions policy; add an sts:ExternalId condition with the value that the vendor gives. Distractors: an IAM user with an access key for the vendor; put the read permissions in the trust policy (trap); let the company choose a shared external ID for all vendors.

Developers launch EC2 instances for one project and must not attach the administrator role. Key: allow iam:PassRole only on the project role ARNs (iam-passrole-prevents-privilege-escalation). Distractors: deny ec2:RunInstances (blocks the work), a permissions boundary on the instances' role only (does not stop passing another role), give developers access keys to place on the instances (trap).

A platform team lets developers create roles for Lambda functions; the roles must never exceed a set maximum. Key: a permissions boundary on the roles (iam-best-practice-boundaries-delegate-role-creation). Distractors: an SCP on the account (limits everyone, sibling-confusion), a boundary that alone is expected to grant (trap), review each role by hand (violates-qualifier). Do not make the key depend on the iam:PermissionsBoundary condition key unless fr-0021 is filled.

Restrict a bucket to all accounts of the organization, now and later. Key: bucket policy with aws:PrincipalOrgID. Distractors: list every account ID (violates-qualifier), Principal * with no condition (trap), a cross-account role in every account.

question_slots.misconception: A request signed with a long-term access key carries MFA information.
question_slots.note: Select TWO. Require MFA before administrators delete objects. Keys: a policy condition on aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent; administrators get temporary credentials with MFA (AssumeRole with MFA or GetSessionToken; iam-mfa-protection-only-with-temporary-credentials). Distractors: rely on the access key alone, S3 MFA Delete for an IAM user (iam-s3-mfa-delete-root-only), aws:SourceIp.

question_slots.misconception: In one account, an IAM allow for kms:Decrypt is enough for any KMS key.
question_slots.note: A company manages its own keys; a role with kms:Decrypt in its IAM policy gets an access denied error on a customer managed key whose key policy names only the key administrators. Key: change the key policy to allow the role or to enable IAM policies (iam-kms-iam-policy-needs-key-policy-permission). Keep KMS detail at the level of this chapter; chapter 06 owns KMS.

question_slots.misconception: One external access analyzer covers resources in every Region.
question_slots.note: Audit which buckets, keys and roles in three Regions are shared outside the organization. Key: IAM Access Analyzer external access analyzers in each Region with the organization as the zone of trust (iam-access-analyzer-external-is-regional, iam-access-analyzer-zone-of-trust). Distractors: one analyzer in one Region, the credential report, the policy simulator.

question_slots.misconception: To reach least privilege you must guess the actions an application uses.
question_slots.note: An application role has AdministratorAccess; the team must replace it with least privilege from what the application really does. Key: Access Analyzer policy generation from CloudTrail activity (iam-access-analyzer-policy-generation-from-cloudtrail). Distractors: the credential report, the policy simulator, an SCP.

Temporary credentials of a role leaked; stop them as soon as possible without breaking new sessions for long. Key: revoke the role's active sessions (iam-revoke-role-sessions-denies-credentials-issued-before). Distractors: revoke the one session token (trap), delete the role (breaks everything), rotate the root access keys.

cards.front: In IAM, the shortest session that AssumeRole accepts is {{c1::900 seconds (15 minutes)}}.
In IAM, a role's maximum session duration setting can be {{c1::1 hour to 12 hours}}.
In AWS STS, role chaining limits a session to {{c1::one hour}}.
In IAM, one AWS account can have at most {{c1::5,000}} IAM users.
In IAM, the root user or an IAM user can register {{c1::up to eight MFA devices}}.
In IAM, one IAM user can have a maximum of {{c1::two access keys}}.
In IAM, trust policy or permissions policy: which one names who can assume the role?
cards.back: The trust policy.

cards.front: In AWS Organizations, can an SCP grant a permission to a role?
cards.back: No. It only sets a ceiling.

cards.front: In IAM, a third-party vendor needs access to your account, MOST secure. What do you use?
cards.back: A cross-account role with an external ID condition.

cards.front: In IAM, same account or cross account: which one needs an allow on both sides?
cards.back: Cross account.

cards.front: In AWS STS, can you revoke one set of temporary credentials?
cards.back: No. Revoke the role's active sessions.

cards.front: In AWS, employees need one sign-in for many accounts, centrally managed. What do you use?
cards.back: IAM Identity Center.

cards.front: In AWS, mobile app users must upload to Amazon S3 with temporary credentials. What do you use?
cards.back: An Amazon Cognito identity pool.

cards.front: In IAM, servers on premises need AWS credentials without long-term keys. What do you use?
cards.back: IAM Roles Anywhere, with certificates from your PKI.

cards.front: In IAM, limit a bucket to every account of your organization, LEAST operational overhead. Which condition key?
cards.back: aws:PrincipalOrgID.

cards.front: In IAM, developers create roles, but the roles must never exceed a set maximum. What do you use?
cards.back: A permissions boundary.

cards.front: In IAM, can you set a permissions boundary for the root user?
cards.back: No. In a member account, use an SCP.

cards.front: In IAM, can one instance profile hold two roles?
cards.back: No. One role per instance profile.

cards.front: In IAM, service role or service-linked role: which one can an administrator edit?
cards.back: The service role.

cards.front: In AWS KMS, can an IAM policy alone allow use of a key whose key policy does not enable IAM policies?
cards.back: No. The key policy must allow it.

cards.front: In IAM, find resources that allow public or cross-account access. What do you use?
cards.back: IAM Access Analyzer, external access.

cards.front: In IAM, build a least-privilege policy from what a role really did. What do you use?
cards.back: Access Analyzer policy generation from CloudTrail.

cards.front: In IAM, does passing a role create a PassRole event in CloudTrail?
cards.back: No. PassRole is a permission, not an API call.

cards.front: In IAM, aws:SourceIp or aws:SourceVpce: which one matches requests through a VPC endpoint?
cards.back: aws:SourceVpce.

cards.front: In IAM, can a user group contain another group?
cards.back: No. Groups cannot be nested.

cards.front: In IAM, does an expired console password stop a user's access keys?
cards.back: No. The access keys keep working.

cards.front: In IAM, bucket policy or cross-account role: which one lets the caller keep its own permissions?
cards.back: The bucket policy (a resource-based policy).

cards.front: In IAM Identity Center, can Active Directory and an external SAML provider be connected at the same time?
cards.back: No. One identity source at a time.

card_plan.rule: Fronts above are drafts for the card writer: keep one fact per card, an answer of at most 12 words, and a display of a fact for any number with a unit.

diagrams.claim: A role gives temporary credentials, and the policies are evaluated each time a request is made.
diagrams.alt: A sequence with three participants: a principal, AWS STS and Amazon S3. The principal asks AWS STS to assume a role. AWS STS checks the trust policy and returns temporary credentials. The principal signs a request to Amazon S3 with them. AWS evaluates the policies, and Amazon S3 returns the object or an access denied error.
say: The principal asks AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) to assume a role.
AWS STS checks that the trust policy of the role names the principal.
AWS STS returns temporary security credentials that expire.
The principal signs a request to Amazon S3 with the temporary credentials.
AWS evaluates the policies that apply, and an explicit deny overrides an explicit allow.
Amazon S3 returns the object, or an access denied error.

diagrams.title: Is the request allowed?
diagrams.claim: A request passes the deny check, every ceiling and one grant, or it is denied.
diagrams.alt: A ladder of four questions. Does any policy explicitly deny the request? Yes ends in an explicit deny. Does an SCP or RCP leave the action out? Does a boundary or session policy leave it out? Is an allow missing from identity-based and resource-based policies? Each of these yes answers ends in an implicit deny. Four answers of no end in allow.

rungs.q: Does any policy explicitly deny the request?
Does an SCP or RCP leave the action out?
Does a boundary or session policy leave it out?
Is an allow missing from identity and resource policies?

diagrams.note: A ladder is a checklist here: only the deny check has a fixed place first (iam-eval-deny-checked-first). The same-account exceptions stay in the frozen Go deeper. Keep the alt at about 60 words (alt text counts toward the file budget).

diagrams.title: Callvale before: one root key
diagrams.claim: One root access key in the code and on three laptops opens the whole account.
diagrams.alt: Before: one EC2 instance runs Callvale's application, which calls Amazon S3 and Amazon Transcribe with the root user's access key. The same key is stored on three laptops. Ana and Ben share the root user's password.
say: The application signs its calls to Amazon S3 and Amazon Transcribe with the root user's access key.
The same access key is stored in the code and on three laptops.
Ana and Ben sign in as the root user with one shared password.
diagrams.note: Story picture: no AWS limit, default or 'can' rule in the labels. Link the caption 'opens the whole account' to iam-root-do-not-create-access-keys (display: full access to all services and resources in the account, including billing information) or reword the caption to state no fact.

diagrams.title: Callvale after: a role for the application
diagrams.claim: The application gets role credentials on the instance, people sign in with MFA, and the root user has no access key.
diagrams.alt: After: an instance profile passes an IAM role to the EC2 instance. The application gets temporary credentials from the instance metadata and calls Amazon S3 and Amazon Transcribe. Ana and Ben sign in as IAM users with MFA in two groups. The root user has MFA and no access key.
say: The instance profile passes the IAM role to the EC2 instance.
The application gets temporary credentials for the role from the instance metadata.
The application calls Amazon S3 and Amazon Transcribe with the temporary credentials.
Ana and Ben sign in as IAM users with MFA, in two groups.
The root user has MFA and no access key.
diagrams.note: No 'IAM role' actor sends credentials: the instance metadata delivers them (exemplar README mistake 10). Keep every component in the same grid cell as in iam-before.
